summary: Defines an administrative framework for SNMPv2 meant to support effective management in a variety of settings. It was an experimental protocol and is now historic.

eli5.summary: A set of house rules for who may talk to which network gadget and how. It was tried out but is no longer used.

questions: what was the snmpv2 administrative framework
how does snmpv2 handle access control
subtitle: A framework for authentication, authorization, and access control in SNMPv2.

tldr.problem: SNMPv2 needs a way to authenticate management requests, authorize users to perform specific operations, and control which management information different users can access.
tldr.mechanism: An administrative framework defines security models (which identify users and apply security algorithms), contexts (scopes of management information), MIB views (subsets of management objects), and access control policies that combine identity, security level, and view permissions.
tldr.outcome: This experimental framework provided a template for security in network management but did not achieve full adoption. Later versions of SNMP built on these ideas.

today: RFC 1909 is Historic. It defined an experimental security and access-control framework for SNMPv2 that provided a template for management protocol security but was superseded by later standards. Modern SNMP implementations use updated security models and frameworks.

sections.title: Introduction and Framework
sections.content:
RFC 1909 defines an administrative framework for SNMPv2, which is a set of rules for how SNMPv2 entities (processes that handle network management messages) can authenticate, authorize, and control access to management information. A typical management domain contains many managed devices (agents), at least one management station, and a management protocol (SNMPv2) that connects them.

The framework describes six key concepts: contexts (scopes of management information, often a physical or logical device), MIB views (subsets of management objects accessible within a context), authentication and privacy (identifying and optionally encrypting messages), security models (the mechanisms that define how security is applied), access control policies (which users can perform which operations on which objects), and proxy (where one agent forwards requests to another).
sections.eli5: A network has many devices. Different people (managers) need to access them. Some people should see everything, some should see only certain things, and some should not be allowed to change anything. This memo explains the rules for that.

sections.title: Contexts, Views, and Access Control
sections.content:
A context is a collection of management information accessible by an SNMPv2 entity. It is typically a single device, but can span multiple devices or part of a device. Each context has a globally unique identification within the management domain. A MIB view is a subset of management objects within a context that an identity is allowed to access. Views are built from view subtrees (sets of objects with a common name prefix) or families (view subtrees parameterized with bitmasks to match groups of similar objects).

An access control policy specifies which operations a particular identity can perform using a particular security level on a particular context. The policy grants two kinds of permissions: a read-view (objects the identity may read) and a write-view (objects the identity may modify). This allows an operator to restrict read access to certain management data and write access to an even smaller set, preventing misuse or accidental damage.
sections.eli5: Some objects on a device show status (read-only), and some can be changed (write). You give each person permission to read certain objects and write to certain others.

sections.title: Security Models, Authentication, and Privacy
sections.content:
A security model defines the mechanisms for achieving a specific level of security. It specifies: how entities are identified (for example, by a username), which authentication and privacy algorithms are used (along with their parameters and keys), how contexts are identified, and how access control policies are derived. The framework notes that authentication and privacy algorithms may change over time as new research or patent issues emerge, so these should be configurable parameters rather than fixed.

The RFC defines that SNMPv2 entities may use different security levels: some messages can be authenticated and encrypted, some authenticated but not encrypted, and some sent with no authentication at all (referred to as "noAuth/noPriv"). This is necessary for management operations that require insecure access, such as discovering previously unknown devices or performing initial synchronization of security keys.
sections.eli5: Some messages should be signed so you know they are real. Some should also be encrypted so nobody can read them. Some do not need either, for things that are not secret.

sections.title: Proxy and Entity Roles
sections.content:
An SNMPv2 agent responds to management requests. It knows about one or more contexts and the management information in each. A proxy SNMPv2 agent forwards requests to other agents based solely on the context, without inspecting the specific management objects being accessed. In contrast, a non-proxy agent inspects the objects and processes requests according to what is being accessed.

An SNMPv2 manager initiates requests on behalf of management applications. An SNMPv2 dual-role entity acts as both manager and agent (initiating some requests and answering others). For a system to be manageable via SNMP, it must have an agent component (even if it also acts as a manager), so the system's own instrumentation can be accessed.
sections.eli5: Some devices answer management questions (agents). Some devices ask other devices questions and pass back the answers (proxies). Some do both (dual-role).

sections.title: Operations and PDU Handling
sections.content:
SNMPv2 defines eight operation types: GetRequest, GetNextRequest, GetBulkRequest, SetRequest, SNMPv2-Trap, Inform, Report, and Response. The framework specifies that access control is checked only when receiving get, get-next, get-bulk, or set operations, and before sending trap or inform notifications. Access control is never checked for response or report operations.

The Report-PDU is a special message sent by an agent when it detects an error in the message "wrapper" (the security layer). Unlike other PDUs, the Report-PDU is not a protocol operation between managers and agents, but rather an error signal between protocol engines. If an agent determines that a received message is unacceptable due to a security problem, it increments a counter and sends a Report-PDU back to the sender.
sections.eli5: There are different kinds of questions and answers. The system checks if you are allowed to ask each kind of question. If something goes wrong with the security wrapper, the device sends an error signal back.
